title: Five ways to draw a literal argument
brief: `pose = estimate(frame, 2.0)` — the 2.0 is not estimate's default, it is a value fed in from outside, like `gain = 2.0; estimate(frame, gain)`. Assuming a pill carries such a source, what goes on it and how could it look? Every direction is drawn on the same run() fixture, with estimate's own default (1.0) present so the two never get confused.
invariants: The literal is a source: data flows out of it into an input port, and which end is the source is judged at the landing (the app's existing rule).
Python grammar on the object: `name = value`, `= value` when unnamed, `= …` when long.
estimate's definition default (`= 1.0`, grey chip) stays on the row; a wired or supplied port dims it.
Prototype-only: HTML/CSS in the app's idiom, nothing in the renderer, no .systemsketch schema change.
boundary: HTML/CSS specimens in the app's idiom — nothing is implemented in the renderer and no .systemsketch schema changed. The state changes, the regenerated code strip and the prune controls are real; editing text, dragging, tooltips and persistence are simulated. The reference board at the top is the real app, driven headlessly.

requirements.name: The picture regenerates one Python program
requirements.why: SystemSketch is a lens over source (the goldens go source.py ↔ target.systemsketch). A drawing that could mean estimate(frame, 2.0), gain = 2.0 + estimate(frame, gain), or estimate(frame) with the default is a bug, not a style.
requirements.passCondition: From the canvas alone, a reader can say which of the three programs the literal regenerates to, without opening an inspector.

anchors.1: A supplied literal and the definition default look the same, or a name changes nothing visible.
anchors.3: Literal and default are distinct, but whether the value is hoisted (named) is ambiguous or lives in two places.
anchors.5: All three states are visibly distinct and the name sits exactly where Python puts it.

requirements.name: No new whiteboard vocabulary
requirements.why: The design rests on tldraw staying stock and on composing from things a whiteboard user already knows (Block, port dot, cable, click-to-edit). Every new gesture is a relearning cost Zach has ruled out.
requirements.passCondition: Every gesture in the direction already exists in the app or in tldraw; only a style value or a command is new.

anchors.1: A new primitive with its own drag, snap, or edit behaviour.
anchors.3: Existing primitives, but one new gesture (a new binding, a dock, a rail) to learn.
anchors.5: Only existing primitives and existing gestures; the new thing is a value of an existing style or one menu command.

requirements.name: Literals do not bury the pipeline
requirements.why: Real calls carry several scalar parameters. If each costs a shape and a cable, decode → estimate → encode disappears under its own arguments — the reason the workflow kit keeps a single-use literal on the row.
requirements.passCondition: Three literal arguments on one Block add at most one row each and no cable that crosses the pipeline.

anchors.1: Every literal always costs a free shape plus a cable.
anchors.3: A shape plus a cable, but compact, or avoidable for the common case.
anchors.5: A single-use literal costs a row or less; shapes appear only when a value is shared or named.

requirements.name: Long values stay legible
requirements.why: A dict or a long string as an argument is common; the sketch already folds it to `= …`. It must never widen a Block or a row, and the whole value must be one gesture away.
requirements.passCondition: A dict literal renders folded and can be read in full without leaving the canvas.

anchors.1: The long value pushes the layout or is simply cut off with no way to read it.
anchors.3: Folded, with the full value only in a tooltip or an inspector.
anchors.5: Folded, with the full value readable in place on demand.

requirements.name: Promotes to a named, shared value in one move
requirements.why: `var = 2.0; estimate(frame, var)` is the refactor in the brief (extract variable). Naming, and then feeding two calls from one source, should be one gesture each and land the name where Python puts it.
requirements.passCondition: A literal can be named in place and its outlet can feed a second consumer without duplicating the value.

anchors.1: No way to name or share without redrawing.
anchors.3: Naming works; sharing requires duplicating the literal or a second step.
anchors.5: Name in place, fan out from the same outlet the port model already has.

hardGates.name: Source ≠ definition default
hardGates.why: The grey `= 1.0` chip on estimate's row is a fact about estimate; the 2.0 is a fact about this call. If they render identically, estimate(frame) and estimate(frame, 1.0) become one picture.

hardGates.name: tldraw stays stock
hardGates.why: Composed only through the Block shape, port, cable/binding, geo and text seams. No forked drag, snap or z-order logic.

hardGates.name: Same fixture, same fidelity
hardGates.why: run() → decode → estimate(frame, 2.0) → encode(pose, {…}) on every hero, with estimate's own default 1.0 present so the gate above is testable.

decisions.label: The object
decisions.value: tldraw's own `oval` geo silhouette with a single outlet dot; text edits like any tldraw text.

decisions.label: Name is the semantics
decisions.value: An unnamed capsule regenerates inline; a named one hoists `name = value` immediately before its first consumer.

decisions.label: Long value
decisions.value: `= …` on the capsule, the full literal in a hover card (touch: tap).

variants.bestWhen: A value is a thing you want to see and point at — a tunable, a constant with a name — and calls have one or two such arguments.
variants.losesWhen: A call has four scalar parameters: four capsules and four cables hide the pipeline the diagram exists to show.
proof: The hero is the shared fixture with the definition default and the supplied literal both visible.
Naming and the long-value card are live states; the code strip regenerates three distinct programs from three distinct pictures.

fr1.evidence: Capsule vs grey chip separates supplied from default; the named state is a different label and a different code line. Three pictures, three programs.

fr2.evidence: Oval, text and cable all exist in stock tldraw and the app; the outlet on a non-Block shape is the one new thing (a port on a geo, or a Block in a capsule view).

fr3.evidence: Every literal is a shape and a cable, always. Compact, but the hero already shows two capsules and two extra cables for two arguments.

fr4.evidence: `= …` keeps the capsule 46px wide; the card shows all three lines of the dict in place.

fr5.evidence: Name by editing the text; the outlet fans out exactly like a Block output already does (fan-out merged 2026-09-01).

g1.evidence: The supplied 2.0 is a separate shape; the definition default stays the grey row chip, dimmed when overridden.

g2.evidence: Oval geo + text + one outlet + the existing cable/binding seam; no new drag or snap logic.

g3.evidence: The hero draws run(), decode, estimate with its 1.0 default, encode with the dict, at the same scale as every other variant.

decisions.label: The object
decisions.value: The existing Block shape with `view: 'value'` — one more value of the view style, no new shape util.

decisions.label: Type on the outlet
decisions.value: The inferred type (`float`, `dict`) shows where a Block shows its kind, so cables can be type-checked by the same judge.

decisions.label: Long value
decisions.value: Preview lines in the body by default; open expands the card, no hover needed.

variants.bestWhen: You want zero new machinery: every Block behaviour (edit, inspect, batch, wire, fan out, save) applies to values the day it ships.
variants.losesWhen: The card is heavier than a capsule; a page of small constants looks like a page of tiny Blocks.
proof: Three live states on the shared fixture; the open dict card shows all three lines in place.
The code strip hoists `gain = 2.0` only in the named state.

fr2.evidence: No new shape, gesture or binding: a Block view value. Everything shown is the Block's existing chrome.

fr3.evidence: A card plus a cable per literal, and the card is larger than a capsule; two arguments already fill the strip under the pipeline.

fr4.evidence: Preview visible with no hover; open state shows the full dict in the body without a floating card.

fr5.evidence: Title edit names it; a Block output already fans out.

g1.evidence: The value card is a separate shape; the definition default stays the grey row chip.

g2.evidence: Adds a value to the existing view style prop; the Block util already renders headings, bodies and ports.

steps.caption: The pill sits on the socket: 2.0 is the argument, nothing else is drawn. A dark dot means 'a plug is in'.

steps.label: Pull it off
steps.caption: Drag it away and it is a free pill with a cable — and it takes the parameter's name, so the code hoists `gain = 2.0`. Drag it back to inline it.

decisions.label: Docked
decisions.value: A pill↔port binding (a new binding type through the BindingUtil seam) keeps the pill flush on the socket; no cable is drawn, and the pill shows only the value (`2.0`, `{…}`) because nothing is being assigned.

decisions.label: Unplug = extract variable
decisions.value: Detaching creates the cable and proposes the parameter's name, so the position of the pill is the inline/hoisted decision.

decisions.label: Sockets
decisions.value: A plugged port dot is dark; a wired one is gold; a default-only one is grey — three dot states.

variants.bestWhen: You want the economy of a row for single-use literals but the same object for shared ones — one pill, two positions.
variants.losesWhen: Docking is a new snap behaviour to learn and to build; a docked pill in the gap between two Blocks is cramped at the current Block spacing.
proof: The docked, unplugged and preview states are live; the pill animates off the socket and the cable appears.
The code strip switches from inline to hoisted only when the pill is off the socket.

fr1.evidence: Docked/unplugged map to inline/hoisted and the default chip stays distinct; but a docked pill that is later renamed has two positions for one program, and the auto-name is a proposal the reader cannot see was accepted.

fr2.evidence: Docking is a new binding and a new drag-off gesture; nothing in the app or in stock tldraw plugs a shape onto a port today.

fr3.evidence: A docked literal costs no cable and no free shape; it still costs a pill-width in the gap before the Block.

fr4.evidence: `= …` folds; the card floats over the neighbouring Block because the docked pill has no room of its own.

fr5.evidence: Naming is the unplug itself; sharing then fans out from the free pill — two gestures rather than one.

g1.evidence: A docked pill is a shape on the socket; the definition default remains the grey chip on the row.

g2.evidence: A new binding type is a supported seam; snapping reuses tldraw's own snap. No engine change, but the gate is passed on the seam, not on zero new code.

g3.evidence: The hero draws run(), decode, estimate with its 1.0 default, encode with the dict, at the same scale as every other variant.

decisions.label: The object
decisions.value: None. The port row gains an editable value field, in the spot the definition-default chip already occupies.

decisions.label: Supplied vs default
decisions.value: Solid field + dark dot = supplied; grey chip + grey dot = default. Wiring a cable hides the field (the kit's rule).

decisions.label: Extract
decisions.value: A context-menu command creates the pill and the cable, proposing the parameter name.

variants.bestWhen: Calls carry many scalar parameters and the pipeline's silhouette matters more than any one value — the common case in an image pipeline.
variants.losesWhen: The row is already tight: at the current Block width the chip alone crowds the name to `g…` (see the reference capture). Shared values need the extract step.
proof: Base, cleared and extracted are live; the dot changes dark → grey → gold with the state.
The code strip shows inline, defaulted and hoisted programs for the three states.

fr1.evidence: Inline, defaulted and hoisted are three pictures and three programs; but supplied-1.0 vs default-1.0 rests on field weight alone on the same row.

fr2.evidence: The kit's own NodeInputRow, in the slot the app's default chip already uses; the only new thing is the Extract command.

fr3.evidence: A literal costs nothing beyond the row it already has; the pipeline strip stays empty.

fr4.evidence: `{…}` fits, but the row has the least room of any direction — the real app already ellipsises `g… fl…` at 340px — and the full value is hover-only.

fr5.evidence: Naming means extracting first; sharing is impossible inline.

g1.evidence: Solid field with a dark dot vs grey chip with a grey dot — distinct, though it is the subtlest pair in the set.

g2.evidence: A field on a row the Block util already lays out; the Extract command composes existing create-shape and connect operations.

g3.evidence: The hero draws run(), decode, estimate with its 1.0 default, encode with the dict, at the same scale as every other variant.

decisions.label: Owner
decisions.value: The enclosing Expanded Block, not the page: the zone is part of run()'s layout, so it moves, collapses and saves with run().

decisions.label: Rows
decisions.value: Each literal is a row with an outlet, sharing the port row's typography and dot; a row feeds any number of consumers.

decisions.label: Long value
decisions.value: `= {…}` on the row, full value on hover; the zone never widens.

variants.bestWhen: You think of a function's constants as its state — the class-family sketch with a state zone on top — and want every literal findable in one place.
variants.losesWhen: Every literal is now far from its consumer, so each needs a cable across the frame; an unnamed row in a zone called locals reads as a variable.
keepParts: locals zone as part of the Expanded layout
proof: Base, named and collapsed are live; collapsing swaps the frame for a Port-view run() with the same two ports.
The code strip hoists `gain = 2.0` only in the named state; collapse is presentational and changes nothing.

fr1.evidence: Row vs grey chip; named row changes the code line; collapse leaves the program untouched. The zone additionally states the scope the literal belongs to.

fr2.evidence: A new region inside the Block's layout with its own rows and outlets — the rows reuse port typography, but the zone itself is a new part of the Block to learn.

fr3.evidence: A literal costs a row (good) plus a cable across the frame to its consumer (the hero shows two cables spanning the strip).

fr4.evidence: `= {…}` keeps the row narrow; the full value is hover-only.

fr5.evidence: Type the name in the row; a row's outlet fans out to as many calls as use it.

g1.evidence: The literal is a row in run()'s zone; the definition default remains the grey chip on estimate's row.

g2.evidence: A layout region inside the existing Block util; outlets use the existing port and cable seams.

g3.evidence: The hero draws run(), decode, estimate with its 1.0 default, encode with the dict, at the same scale as every other variant.

checks: Exactly five structural directions on the where-it-lives / who-owns-it axes
Same run() fixture, same definition default, same scale on every hero
Visual atlas before the score audit; no winner cue in the atlas
Every hero has a three-step story with live direct controls on the same states
Five weighted FRs and three gates frozen before the previews were built; weights sum to 100
Every score carries evidence and a confidence
Reference board is the real app driven headlessly, plus the sketches from the brief
defaultWhy: Value Block leads at 84/100, a fragile margin over Capsule at 83: it is the same Block primitive wearing a fourth view, so click-to-edit, the inspector, batch styles, fan-out and the file format apply to values the day it ships, and a long value has a body to live in. The Capsule silhouette from your sketch can simply be what that view looks like.
decisionHinge: The order is decided by how much weight 'literals do not bury the pipeline' carries. At 20% the two free-shape directions lead; raise it to 30% (taking 10 from vocabulary) and Inline literal (V4) moves to the top at ~83 while Value Block drops to ~80 — which is the workflow kit's own answer. The strongest splice is therefore V2's model with V4's row as the docked, single-use form: a value is a Block, but an unnamed literal with one consumer is allowed to live on the row until you name or share it.
